one_liner: Intel's C++ classical-ML library (k-means, SVM, kNN, linear models, PCA) behind sklearnex; beats stock scikit-learn on multi-core x86.
what_it_does: oneDAL implements classical machine-learning algorithms for dense tabular data (k-means, DBSCAN, kNN, SVM, linear, ridge and logistic regression, random forests, PCA, basic statistics) for CPUs, Intel GPUs via SYCL, and MPI clusters. Its C++ API is its own: build a descriptor, then call dal::train / dal::infer on dal::table objects. Most users reach it through the Python Extension for Scikit-learn (sklearnex), whose patch_sklearn() routes supported estimator and parameter combinations to oneDAL and silently falls back to stock scikit-learn for the rest.
how_it_is_fast: Each kernel is compiled for SSE2, AVX2 and AVX-512 and picked at runtime, data is processed in cache-sized blocks on a oneTBB-based threading layer, and the heavy arithmetic is cast as oneMKL BLAS/LAPACK calls. SVM training uses a ThunderSVM-style working-set SMO solver with an LRU kernel cache, and SVM prediction computes test-row by support-vector kernel blocks as matrix-matrix products instead of libsvm's per-sample loop. Linear regression accumulates X^T X and X^T y and solves the normal equations by Cholesky (eigendecomposition pseudo-inverse fallback) instead of scikit-learn's SVD-based scipy.linalg.lstsq. Against stock scikit-learn, much of the gain is simply using every core where scikit-learn (libsvm) runs single-threaded.
when_to_use: Existing scikit-learn code on a many-core Intel Xeon using SVC, SVR, NuSVC or NuSVR (vendor chart: fit 11.7-28.8x, predict 236-396x on 64 cores), kd_tree kNN predict (138-153x), KMeans (fit 7.7x, predict 24.6x) or Ridge fit (15.2x).
Tall dense least-squares or ridge problems (hundreds of thousands to millions of rows, tens to thousands of features) whose X^T X is well conditioned.
C++ services that need classical ML without Python, with batch, online and distributed (MPI/SPMD) modes in one library.
Offloading the same scikit-learn estimators to Intel GPUs via SYCL (sklearnex config_context(target_offload='gpu:0')).
when_not_to_use: Lasso and ElasticNet (1.1-1.2x), brute-force kNN fit (1.0x) or PCA fit (1.7x): the vendor's own chart shows little gain.
Sparse matrices, sample_weight, positive=True, ball_tree kNN or non-lloyd KMeans: sklearnex falls back to stock scikit-learn for these (its algorithms page lists the conditions).
Ill-conditioned least squares where you need the SVD-based accuracy of scipy lstsq, or results bit-identical to scikit-learn; sklearnex promises only 'equivalent mathematical accuracy'.
Non-Intel CPUs and Arm CPUs without SVE: every published number is on Intel Xeon, and the Arm backend has no NEON path (binaries require SVE).
Single-core or latency-bound jobs, where the share of the speedup that comes from 64-way threading shrinks.

integration.form: shared lib (static libs also built; Python users install the scikit-learn-intelex wheel or conda package)
integration.dependencies: oneTBB, oneMKL (or the OpenBLAS reference backend), oneDPL; DPC++ compiler plus oneMKL for SYCL/GPU builds; MPI or oneCCL for distributed samples
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (makefile compiles with -std=c++17); Intel ICX is the default compiler, GCC, Clang and MSVC 2022 also supported; clang-cl from LLVM 22.1.8+ on Windows arm64; sklearnex supports Python 3.10-3.14 and scikit-learn 1.6-1.9
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux and Windows (runtime dispatch SSE2, AVX2, AVX-512); Linux aarch64 and Windows arm64 SVE-only; riscv64 listed as a makefile platform; Intel GPUs via SYCL; MPI clusters
integration.thread_safety: not documented in the pages read; internal parallelism runs on a oneTBB-based threading layer whose API is internal
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — patch_sklearn() keeps the scikit-learn API for supported estimator/parameter combinations and silently falls back otherwise; the C++ API is a separate descriptor/train/infer interface

gotchas: Fallback is silent: unsupported parameters or inputs run stock scikit-learn, and only the INFO-level 'sklearnex' logger shows 'running accelerated version on' versus 'fallback to original Scikit-learn'. Turn that logger on before trusting a speedup.

LinearRegression swaps the algorithm: oneDAL solves the normal equations by Cholesky with a hard-coded 1e-6 diagonal cutoff (the source comment calls the thresholds 'just a guess') and falls back to an eigendecomposition pseudo-inverse, while scikit-learn 1.8 calls SVD-based scipy.linalg.lstsq. The 48.5x fit bar therefore partly measures a cheaper, less stable method. Ridge (15.2x) is the like-for-like comparison, since scikit-learn's 'auto' solver on dense data is also Cholesky.

Harness asymmetries in IntelPython/scikit-learn_bench: the SVM rows pit 64-thread oneDAL against single-threaded libsvm, so with perfect scaling the per-core gain would be only about 3.7-6.2x for SVC/SVR/NuSVC/NuSVR predict (derived from page data). The 'physical_cpus' n_jobs value comes from psutil.cpu_count(logical=False), which counts all 128 cores of the two-socket host even though the run was bound to 64 with numactl, so the kNN baselines probably ran oversubscribed. configs/common/linear_model.json also puts the scikit-learn n_jobs, solver and tol settings outside 'algorithm', so they are silently ignored; that is harmless with scikit-learn 1.8 defaults. The datasets behind each bar are in an unpublished 'backup'.

Open correctness bugs: oneDAL #3820 (opened 2026-09-29) reports that the multinomial cross_entropy_loss value and gradient vary between calls at 4+ threads (relative error up to 1.1e-4 and 7.2e-3), which makes L-BFGS stop early; the reporter saw test log loss degrade from 0.603 to 0.763 with sklearnex 2026.1.0 and suspects the AVX2 path. #3329 reports an OpenBLAS-backend race on the global BLAS thread count.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: mlpack is the catalogued sibling that is also measured against scikit-learn (k-NN and k-means in its paper). Pick oneDAL when you want to keep scikit-learn code unchanged on Intel x86, or need SVM and linear models with GPU or MPI modes from a vendor-maintained library. CatBoost covers gradient-boosted-tree inference, which this chart does not test. The deep-learning siblings (FlashAttention, oneDNN Graph Compiler, LIBXSMM) target different workloads.
verified_claims_summary: Intel ran its scikit-learn_bench harness on one socket (64 physical cores, numactl-bound) of a two-socket Xeon 6767P, comparing stock scikit-learn 1.8.0 with sklearnex 2026.0.0 using prebuilt packages (no compiler flags given). It reports combined FP32/FP64 speedups (the harness's report tool aggregates by geometric mean) from 1.0x (brute kNN fit) to 48.5x (LinearRegression fit) for training and from 1.1x (Lasso, ElasticNet) to 395.8x (NuSVR predict) for inference, against README text of '8.5x average' and 'up to 100X'. The separate Spark chart (DAAL 2020 via OAP MLlib against Spark MLlib 2.4.4 on 7 x m5.2xlarge, double precision) shows 3.6-18.2x.
status_note: Actively maintained under the UXL Foundation (last commit 2026-10-06, 2026.x releases) and Apache-2.0. The build is heavy (Intel make/Bazel plus oneTBB and oneMKL), so most users take the conda, NuGet or pip packages. The Spark path in the README, OAP MLlib, was archived on 2026-07-06 with a notice that Intel will not support it and that it has known security issues.
